title: Go to the ant (Proverbs 6:6–11)
hook: the ant has no boss, yet stores food in summer
carry: a little folding of the hands

segments.voice: Yesterday, the beginning of wisdom and a walking stick that might snap. Your line was lean not on your own. Did you say I don't know, and mean it? Day four hundred fifty-one.

Late summer, on a dry hillside in the land of Israel. Look down at the path and there's a line of ants, each one carrying a seed bigger than its head. Down a hole they go, and up they come empty, and back out to the grass for another. Below ground there are chambers packed with grain, stored against the winter. Nobody is shouting orders. No ant is standing at the top with a clipboard. They just work, in the season for working. Someone in ancient Israel crouched down and watched this for a long time. And then wrote it up, as a lesson for a person still in bed.
screen: `A LINE OF ANTS ON A HILLSIDE.` → `SEEDS BIGGER THAN THEIR HEADS.` → `NOBODY GIVING ORDERS.`

segments.voice: Proverbs chapter six, in the King James Bible: "Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise: Which having no guide, overseer, or ruler, provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest." A sluggard is someone who keeps putting things off. And the teacher here is tiny. No guide, overseer, or ruler. That's a sharp piece of observation. Biologists say an ant colony does have a queen, but she lays eggs; she doesn't give orders. The work gets done without a boss. And the seed-storing detail is real too. In that region, harvester ants carry seeds underground and keep them in granaries. Then the teacher turns to the person in bed. "How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep? Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep." Hear the rhythm of that. It's not one huge decision to be lazy. It's a little more. Just a little. Five more minutes, hit snooze. And then: "So shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth, and thy want as an armed man." Not slowly. Like a traveler arriving at the door, like a robber. Two cautions, because Proverbs isn't a boot camp. The same Bible commands a day of rest every week, and the ant itself works in its season, not every hour. And elsewhere Proverbs suggests that the poor can lose their harvest to injustice, not idleness. This saying is about one thing: the small, repeated delay. The ant doesn't wait to be told. It sees the season, and it moves.
screen: `NO GUIDE, OVERSEER, OR RULER` · `SEEDS STORED UNDERGROUND` · `A LITTLE SLEEP, A LITTLE SLUMBER` · `WORK IN SEASON, REST IN SEASON` · then, large: `GO TO THE ANT, THOU SLUGGARD; CONSIDER HER WAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: finish one small job before resting. Before the sit, choose one small thing you've been putting off. A dish in the sink. An email that needs one line. A bill. A drawer. Something that takes five minutes or less. For the sit, picture yourself doing it, start to finish, without a boss telling you to. Notice where you'd usually say, just a little later. If you pray, you can ask for help to do the next small thing. If you don't, simply set the intention. Then, when the bell rings, go and do it, and rest after. The bell holds the time.
Sluggard. Proverbs' name for the person who keeps putting things off, sent to watch an ant with no boss working all summer.
Your line: a little folding of the hands. Today, the next time you hear yourself say just a little later, do the small thing now instead. Day four hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Christians often teach Proverbs 6:6–11 to children and young people as a lesson in diligence, alongside the weekly Sabbath or Lord's Day rest that keeps work in its place.

options: wait for someone to tell you what to do.
fork.reveal: "which having no guide, overseer, or ruler, provideth her meat in the summer." the ant moves in the season, without being told.

original.note: Hebrew: ant. it appears only twice in the Bible, both times in Proverbs.

trapdoor: what you thought: a stern saying about working harder.
what it means: a lesson from a tiny creature that works in its season without a boss, and a warning about 'just a little' more delay.
what a scholar hears: the observation fits harvester ants that store seed underground; and Proverbs 13:23 adds that poverty can come from injustice.

notes: Biology: queen ants lay eggs and do not direct work; harvester ants (Messor species) in the region store seeds in underground granaries. Confirm phrasing.
